title: Uptake of the COVID-19 vaccine and its association with vaccine information and misinformation in Malawi
screen_reason: Cross-sectional survey of 895 Malawian adults that asked, for each of ten researcher-selected COVID-19 and COVID-19-vaccine conspiracy statements, whether the respondent had heard it. The paper reports the share of respondents who had heard specific statements (80.7% and 74.1%) and the median number of the ten heard, with the 895-respondent denominator stated. Self-reported encountering of misinformation with a denominator, so RECALL (exposure). Belief in the statements is also reported but belief is outside the review's scope and is not extracted.

estimates.platform: face-to-face interviewer-administered survey at health facilities
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who reported having heard the conspiracy statement 'The spread of COVID-19 is a deliberate attempt to reduce the size of the global population'
estimates.denominator: 895 Malawian adults aged 18 and over attending the outpatient, non-communicable disease or HIV clinic at one of 32 Partners in Hope-supported health facilities across all three regions of Malawi
estimates.definition: respondent answered that they had heard this statement, one of ten common circulating conspiracy statements about COVID-19 and the COVID-19 vaccine read out by the interviewer
estimates.misinfo_def: "Exposure to COVID-19 misinformation was characterized by counting how many statements (here classified as conspiracy theories) each respondent had heard"
estimates.source_quote: Respondents reported having heard a median of 5 of the 10 surveyed conspiracy theories. The most commonly heard were “The spread of COVID-19 is a deliberate attempt to reduce the size of the global popula- tion”(80.7%ofrespondents[SE16.2])and“TheCOVID-19virusisahoax” (74.1% of respondents) [SE 15.7] (Fig. 3, Supplementary Data 2).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines', opening paragraph (run-together words are a PDF rendering artefact); Fig. 3 and Supplementary Data 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure is self-reported: the respondent said whether they had heard each statement. Falsity itself was not judged by the respondent but fixed in advance by the investigators, who put ten statements they classify as conspiracy theories, drawn from documented circulating claims in Malawi (refs 30, 31). Coded self_report because the measurement of exposure is the respondent's own report; no coder-reliability statistic applies. Instrument developed in English, translated to Chichewa and checked by bilingual team members.
estimates.moderator_quote: We asked whether the respondents had heard each of ten common statements (circulating conspiracy theories in Malawi) about COVID-19 and the COVID-19 vaccine. ... Fig. 3 | Prevalence of COVID-19 conspiracy theory beliefs across demographics. Heat map displaying the percentage of survey respondents (overall, by gender, and by place of residence) who reported hearing of 10 common COVID-19 conspiracies (n = 895)
estimates.notes: This is the single most-heard of the ten statements, so it is a ceiling and not a representative rate of misinformation exposure; the median respondent had heard 5 of the 10 (separate row). The reported SE of 16.2 percentage points is implausible for a proportion of 0.807 at n = 895 (binomial SE would be about 1.3 points) even allowing for facility-level clustering, and the same problem appears for the second statement (SE 15.7); the point estimates are used and the SEs are not. sampling_frame coded convenience because respondents are care-seekers at 32 purposively chosen facilities, sampled systematically within the clinic queue rather than from any population frame; an adjudicator preferring survey_sample for interviewer-administered surveys would be defensible.

estimates.notes: An intensity, not a proportion: value_pct carries the count 5, bounded by the ten-item instrument, so it is not comparable with per-capita counts from open-ended or behavioural measures. The paper gives a median only; no overall mean is reported (subgroup means are: men 5.51, women 4.76; urban 5.70, rural 4.95; secondary-or-higher 5.85, primary-or-less 4.79). borderline=true because whether a bounded item-battery count belongs in the intensity pool is a review-level decision.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Belief measures were deliberately not extracted, per the exclusion of belief in false claims: 72% of respondents believed none of the ten statements; among the 254 who believed any, an average of two; item-level endorsement of 22.7%, 17.3%, 16.9%, 15.2%, 10.7%, 8.4%, 5.5% in Table 2. Note that Table 2's endorsement column is internally inconsistent (134 = 22.7%, but 73 = 17.3% and 122 = 16.9% cannot both hold on the same denominator, and none of these matches n = 895), which is a further reason not to use it. 2) Tone-of-information figures were not extracted because negative tone is anti-vaccine framing, not a falsity judgement: about one-fifth of those exposed via social media and messaging apps, 41% of those exposed via traditional medicine practitioners and just over 10% of those exposed via peers or family called the information negative in tone; women rated on average 10.2% of their sources negative versus 7.6% for men. If the review counts 'perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment', these are the candidate rows, but they measure perceived tone of vaccine information rather than perceived misinformation. 3) Source-exposure shares (over 90% for friends/neighbours, health workers and radio; 3% for traditional medicine practitioners; roughly one-quarter to one-third for social media, messaging apps, television or newspapers) are exposure to vaccine information in general, not to misinformation. 4) Vaccination uptake (43% with at least one dose), trust in sources (69.4% a health care provider) and all odds ratios are outcome and association measures, not prevalence. 5) The background figures 'approximately 1 in 4 people have received a COVID-19 vaccination' and '22% had completed the primary series as of December 2023' are cited from other sources and barred by R8. 6) The remaining eight item-level exposure percentages sit in Fig. 3's heat map and Supplementary Data 2 and cannot be read from this text file.

rob.design: Cross-sectional interviewer-administered survey, May-June 2022, at 32 Partners in Hope-supported public and faith-based health facilities chosen to span urban, peri-urban and rural areas in all three Malawian regions. Eligible: adults 18+, attending the outpatient, NCD or HIV clinic, not acutely ill. Systematic random sampling of every second person in the provider queue. AAPOR Response Rate 3 = 95.1%: 944 approached, 3 screened out as under 18, 46 declined screening or consent, 895 completed (mean interview 29 minutes). Instrument written in English, translated into Chichewa and reviewed by bilingual team members; administered privately by trained research assistants on SurveyCTO tablets; 4,000 kwacha (about US$5) incentive. Analysis in Stata 17 with svyset clustering at the facility level. Ethics: Malawi NHSRC #2883 and UCLA IRB #22-000380. Powered for a different primary question (a 5-point difference in vaccination coverage by HIV status). Main limitations for prevalence use: the frame is health-facility attendees rather than the general population; exposure is self-reported recognition of ten investigator-chosen statements, so it is bounded by the item list and open to acquiescence and recall error; the reported standard errors on the item percentages are implausibly large.
